points.label: What a dataset is
points.description: The learner states that a dataset is a collection of examples (rows, samples, or instances) gathered for the model to learn from, and gives at least one concrete example such as images, emails, or measurements.

points.label: Structure: examples and attributes
points.description: The learner explains that each example in a dataset is described by the same set of attributes (columns, fields, or features), so the dataset can be pictured as a table where rows are examples and columns are attributes.

points.label: Quality and representativeness matter
points.description: The learner states that a model can only learn patterns that are present in its dataset, so the dataset must be large enough and representative of the situations the model will face; biased, noisy, or unrepresentative data leads to bad predictions.

misconceptions.summary: More data is always better, so any extra rows automatically improve the model.
misconceptions.correction: The learner explains that data quality and representativeness matter as much as quantity: adding mislabeled, duplicated, or unrepresentative rows can hurt the model, so extra data only helps when it is relevant and correctly reflects the target population.

misconceptions.summary: A dataset is just whatever the model outputs after it has been trained.
misconceptions.correction: The learner clarifies that the dataset is the input to training, collected before or independently of the model; the model's outputs are predictions, not the dataset itself.

beginner: So a dataset is just... a big file? What is actually inside it?
If I wanted to build a model that recognizes cats in photos, what would my dataset need to contain?
confident: I'm pretty sure that if I just collect a million rows of any data, my model will be great — size is all that matters.
A dataset and a database are the same thing, right? Any database can be used to train a model as-is.
skeptic: If my dataset only contains photos taken in daylight, why should I trust the model at night? Doesn't that make the whole approach fragile?
How do you even know a dataset is representative? Isn't 'representative' just a word people use after the fact?
